findings.title: Double concurrency cap: yf internal queue AND worker pool both = PULL_CONCURRENCY
findings.description: The yahoo-finance2 client is constructed with queue.concurrency = _YF_CONC (PULL_CONCURRENCY, default 10), and runWorkerPool is launched with CONCURRENCY = PULL_CONCURRENCY (also 10). The worker pool spawns 10 workers, but each processOne issues MANY HTTP calls (quoteSummary fans out to ~14 modules in one call, plus yf.quote for IPO date, plus fetchFundamentalsTS makes 4 sequential FTS calls). All of these are funneled through the single yf queue whose global cap is also 10. So 10 workers compete for 10 global HTTP slots, where one worker's FTS step alone wants 4 sequential slots; workers spend most of their time blocked in the yf queue rather than the worker-pool sleep. The two limits are coupled to the same env var, so raising PULL_CONCURRENCY to get more workers ALSO raises the global HTTP cap proportionally — there is no independent throttle. Effective HTTP parallelism is min(workers, yfQueue) = PULL_CONCURRENCY, but the per-worker rateLimitMs sleep (1500ms) is applied on top, so real throughput is far below the documented '13 tickers/sec'.
findings.mechanism: Worker count and yf-queue concurrency both derive from PULL_CONCURRENCY, so they cannot be tuned independently; the per-ticker multi-call fan-out (1 quoteSummary + 1 quote + up to 4 FTS) saturates the shared queue while workers also each sleep rateLimitMs, compounding the throttle.
findings.reproducer: Set PULL_CONCURRENCY=20 expecting 2x HTTP parallelism; the yf queue now also allows 20 concurrent, raising Yahoo 429 rate while worker sleeps stay at 1500ms — throughput does not scale linearly and 429s increase.
findings.impact: Tuning is a blunt instrument: the only knob simultaneously changes worker count, global HTTP cap, and thus 429 exposure. The 165-min CI step budget is hard to hit predictably; raising concurrency to finish faster directly worsens the rate-limit storms the retry logic exists to absorb.
findings.suggested_fix: Decouple the two: introduce a separate YF_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY env, or set yf queue.concurrency = CONCURRENCY exactly so each worker holds one global slot and FTS's 4 calls run sequentially within it. Make the worker-pool sleep the single rate governor.

findings.title: Worker-pool inter-ticker sleep keyed on shared idx, not myIdx — tail workers skip throttle
findings.description: In runWorkerPool, each worker reads const myIdx = idx++ (safe: no await between read and increment, so atomic on the single-threaded loop). But the throttle at the end of the loop is `if (idx < stocks.length) await _sleep(sleepMs)` — it tests the SHARED idx, not myIdx. Because idx has already been advanced by every other worker that grabbed a ticket, idx reaches stocks.length while up to CONCURRENCY-1 tickers are still being processed. Those final in-flight tickers then skip their rateLimitMs sleep entirely. The sleep is meant to be a per-worker gate, but gating on global idx makes the pacing condition reflect global queue position rather than this worker's own remaining work, so steady-state pacing degrades near the tail of every run.
findings.mechanism: idx is shared mutable state advanced by all workers; using it (rather than the worker's own myIdx or an unconditional sleep) for the throttle decision means the last CONCURRENCY-1 tickers race without delay once idx hits length.
findings.reproducer: Run with a watchlist of N where N mod CONCURRENCY != 0 and instrument the sleep — the final CONCURRENCY-1 full-pull tickers issue back-to-back with no rateLimitMs gap, occasionally tripping a 429 at end-of-run.
findings.impact: Rate-limit pressure spikes at the tail of each run; pacing is not uniform, undermining the deterministic-throttle assumption the retry budgets were tuned against. Not corrupting.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the `idx < stocks.length` guard and sleep unconditionally (the next loop iteration breaks on myIdx>=length anyway), or gate on this worker: `if (myIdx + concurrency < stocks.length) await _sleep(sleepMs)`.

findings.title: Legacy incomeStatementHistory empty since Nov 2024; FTS is sole source with no backstop
findings.description: The mapper builds annualRev/annualOpInc/annualNetIncome/annualGP and revenueQ/opIncQ/grossProfitQ from yahoo.incomeStatementHistory(.Quarterly). The code's own comment (line 1003) and the suppressed yf warning (line 76) state these legacy quoteSummary submodules 'have provided almost no data since Nov 2024'. In practice the entire quoteSummary-derived annual/quarterly block is near-empty for most tickers and snapshots depend ENTIRELY on the FTS merge. The QS-vs-FTS 'strictly more non-null entries' gates (lines 1837-1839, 1846-1848) reduce to 'FTS always wins'. The Tag 202 'quoteSummary is the primary RnD source' logic (annualRnDFromQS, line 632) reads the same dead submodule, so it is effectively always empty and FTS is the real primary despite the comment. There is no working fallback if FTS field names drift.
findings.mechanism: Yahoo deprecated incomeStatementHistory data in Nov 2024; the mapper still reads it (gets [] for most tickers) and silently relies on FTS as sole source, so the supposed QS fallback/primary paths are dead and any FTS drift empties fundamentals universe-wide with no backstop.
findings.reproducer: Pull NVDA and inspect canonical.annual.annualRev before the FTS merge — length 0 / all-null. Confirm annualRnDFromQS is all-null for ASML/V/MA, so only the FTS branch ever populates RnD.
findings.impact: Single point of failure on FTS. Any FTS field-name drift silently empties annual/quarterly fundamentals across the whole universe; the suppressed warning hides it. Methods depending on annual.* go computable:false en masse with no obvious alarm.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-run sentinel counting tickers whose annual.annualRev is non-empty post-merge; assert it stays above a floor (e.g. >80% of attempted) and fail/alert if it collapses, turning the silent FTS dependency into a monitored invariant.

findings.title: FTS field-name lists are hardcoded live-probe guesses; rename yields silent null
findings.description: _ftsValue tries an explicit camelCase key list then a generated snake_case variant (k.replace(/[A-Z]/g,'_'+lower)). The candidate lists are hand-maintained against live probes (comments cite 'verified live against NVDA'). When Yahoo renames or splits an FTS field (the documented Nov-2024-class drift), the lookup silently returns null and the value vanishes with no thrown error — data-quality erosion, not an exception. At-risk fields: sellingGeneralAndAdministration (SGA → Beneish/Ohlson), depreciationAndAmortization, dilutedAverageShares (buyback-yield), operatingCashFlow, freeCashFlow. The snake_case generator also will not match acronym/&-style renames. A rename degrades the dependent method to computable:false universally — exactly the failure mode this file's history (Tag 211l, Tag 219) keeps re-discovering by manual probe.
findings.mechanism: FTS extraction relies on exact-string key matching against an evolving schema; a rename produces a valid-looking null (not an error), so affected fields silently disappear from snapshots without tripping the mapper-bug or fail-ratio gates.
findings.reproducer: Rename an expected FTS key in a fixture (operatingCashFlow → cashFlowFromContinuingOperatingActivities); annualOCF goes all-null and reinvestment-rate/Ohlson lose coverage with zero CI signal.
findings.impact: Slow silent decay of method coverage as Yahoo drifts; no alarm because nulls are valid. Each occurrence historically required a manual live-probe audit to discover.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit a per-run FTS field-coverage report (% non-null per logical field across attempted tickers) into the manifest and gate on a sharp drop for any previously well-populated field.

findings.title: Schema-validation errors classified as not-found, auto-marking live intl tickers delisted
findings.description: The errClass switch maps /Failed Yahoo Schema validation|schema validation/i to 'not-found' (line 2097), and the not-found branch (line 2101) opens the existing snapshot and sets meta.delisted=true + delistedAt. The code comment acknowledges the risk: 'if Yahoo ever introduces a real schema break we'd silently re-classify it as not-found'. This conflates a genuine delisting with the yahoo-finance2 strict-shape validator rejecting a partially-populated-but-valid response. Run #107 already produced 637 such failures, all on international tickers. If a yahoo-finance2 version bump or a Yahoo additive-field change makes the validator reject a whole region's live tickers, every one gets stamped delisted in its snapshot — and delisted snapshots are typically excluded downstream. The 'monitor the schema-vs-not-found ratio' mitigation is described but not implemented here.
findings.mechanism: A library-validation failure (transient, version/schema-coupled) is bucketed identically to a permanent symbol-not-found, and that bucket has a side effect (mark delisted) persisted into the snapshot, so a validator regression silently delists live securities region-wide.
findings.reproducer: Bump yahoo-finance2 to a version with a stricter schema for one region, run the pull; affected live tickers acquire meta.delisted=true despite trading normally.
findings.impact: Whole regions of live tickers can be silently delisted and dropped from scoring on a library/schema change, shrinking the universe with no fail-ratio signal (not-found is not a hard failure).
findings.suggested_fix: Give schema-validation its own errClass ('schema-reject') that does NOT set meta.delisted, and add a CI gate that fails when schema-reject count exceeds a small threshold or concentrates in one region. Only literal 'No data found / Quote not found' should mark delisted.

findings.title: Manifest flush cadence keyed on per-worker myIdx; SIGKILL can leave n_ok undercounted
findings.description: writeManifestIncremental's boolean mutex + _manifestPending re-trigger machinery is effectively dead for the synchronous writeFileAtomic path (it sets and clears _manifestWriting within one tick, so no other worker can interleave; the setImmediate re-trigger only matters if the write were async). The real exposure: flushes fire at `myIdx % 100 === 0` using the worker's LOCAL myIdx (line 2139). Because tickets are grabbed concurrently and processing time varies, the '100-ticker cadence' is irregular and the only guaranteed up-to-date write is the post-loop final flush (line 2147). If the process is SIGKILLed at the 165-min CI cap between the last %100 flush and the final flush, the on-disk partial manifest can undercount n_ok by up to ~100+CONCURRENCY snapshots that were actually written, and Verify Pull Coverage reads a stale-low n_ok.
findings.mechanism: Flush cadence is driven by per-worker myIdx modulo, not a global processed counter, and there is no SIGTERM/SIGKILL flush; a mid-run kill leaves the manifest lagging the actual on-disk snapshot count.
findings.reproducer: SIGKILL the process at minute 164 mid-run; compare _manifest.json n_ok to the count of *.json snapshot files on disk — n_ok is lower because the last partial window never flushed.
findings.impact: Coverage gate can see an undercounted n_ok after a timeout-kill, failing CI on a run that actually wrote enough snapshots (or masking the inverse via skipped-mcap accounting).
findings.suggested_fix: Drive the cadence off a shared processed counter (`if (++done % 100 === 0)`), and trap SIGTERM to flush the manifest once before exit so the on-disk count matches reality at kill time.

findings.title: FTS fetch leg has no 429 retry; rate-limit there fails ticker despite quoteSummary backoff
findings.description: quoteSummaryWithRetry retries on isRateLimit OR isTimeout with a 15s/45s/90s ladder. But the FTS path (line 1776) wraps fetchFundamentalsTS in one _withAbortTimeout (60s for 4 sequential internal calls) and only retries when attempt===0 AND (message includes 'timeout' OR code==='ECONNRESET'). There is NO 429/rate-limit check in the FTS retry condition. So under a Yahoo throttle, quoteSummary may succeed on retry while the subsequent FTS calls 429 straight through, immediately throwing 'FTS fetch failed' and failing the whole ticker — discarding the successful quoteSummary work. Separately, _withAbortTimeout fires ac.abort() then rejects with its own ETIMEDOUT; the aborted underlying yahoo-finance2 promise rejects later with an AbortError that is no longer awaited (Promise.race already settled), an unhandled-rejection candidate that could crash under --unhandled-rejections=strict.
findings.mechanism: Retry policy is inconsistent across the two fetch sites: quoteSummary retries 429+timeout with long backoff; the FTS sibling retries only timeout/ECONNRESET once and ignores 429, so a rate-limit during the FTS leg fails the ticker outright.
findings.reproducer: Throttle Yahoo so quoteSummary succeeds on retry but the FTS calls 429; the ticker logs 'FTS fetch failed' with no FTS backoff attempted, despite a good quoteSummary.
findings.impact: Elevated full-pull failure rate during throttling concentrated on the FTS leg, plus wasted quoteSummary calls. Inflates n_failed and 429 churn precisely when the system should be backing off.
findings.suggested_fix: Add 429/rate-limit detection to the FTS retry condition with the same backoff ladder, and attach a no-op .catch to the aborted underlying promise to avoid unhandled-rejection exposure.

findings.title: FX_TO_USD seeded from raw.rates verbatim casing but always read uppercased; stale-revert gap
findings.description: loadFx initializes FX_TO_USD = Object.assign({}, FX_FALLBACK, raw.rates), copying raw.rates keys VERBATIM, while _convertToUSD and _convertSnapshotToUSD always look up by currency.toUpperCase(). The per-currency staleness loop only operates on FX_TO_USD[up] (uppercased). Consistency holds today only because refresh-fx happens to emit uppercase currency codes — an invariant enforced nowhere. If refresh-fx, a manual edit, or a future provider ever writes a lowercase/mixed-case rate key, line 171 stores it lowercase; the stale-revert branch deletes only FX_TO_USD[up] (line 200) leaving the lowercase duplicate intact, so a stale rate could survive under the lowercase key while provenance reports fallback. The coupling is undocumented and fragile.
findings.mechanism: FX rate keys are stored with provider casing in one path (Object.assign) but always read uppercased; the per-currency stale-revert only touches the uppercased key, so a lowercase duplicate bypasses the staleness gate.
findings.reproducer: Hand-edit fx-rates.json adding lowercase 'try':0.029 with metadata marking it stale; the stale-revert deletes FX_TO_USD['TRY'] but 'try' persists and provenance is inconsistent.
findings.impact: Latent: a casing change in the FX provider silently bypasses the per-currency staleness gate, applying stale EM rates while snapshots report fallback provenance — mispriced EM legs without alarm.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize keys to uppercase at load: build FX_TO_USD by iterating raw.rates and assigning FX_TO_USD[k.toUpperCase()] = rate, never Object.assign of raw verbatim; assert all keys uppercase after load.

findings.title: refresh-universe screener sweep fully sequential and untimed — hang risk, slow
findings.description: The universe refresh iterates REGIONS (25) x SCREENER_IDS (13) = 325 sequential fetchScreener calls each followed by await _sleep(300), then EXCHANGE_CODES (29) with paginated sequential fetchExchangePage calls (await _sleep(400) per page). It is entirely serial with no per-call timeout (unlike pull-yahoo's _withAbortTimeout). A single hung yf.screener socket stalls the whole refresh indefinitely with nothing to cancel it. The 300/400ms inter-call sleeps alone sum to well over a minute of pure sleeping. The architecture is also inconsistent: the cheap auth-free discovery fetches run in parallel (Promise.allSettled, lines 323-330) but the expensive Yahoo screener sweep is strictly serial and unbounded-time.
findings.mechanism: The screener/exchange sweep uses sequential await with fixed sleeps and no timeout; one hung yf.screener call has nothing to abort it, so the refresh can stall and otherwise runs far slower than necessary.
findings.reproducer: Simulate one region's yf.screener never resolving (network black hole); refresh-universe hangs forever on that region, never reaching the exchange/discovery phases.
findings.impact: Slow refresh and a hang-risk single point of failure; in CI a hung screener call eats the whole job budget and new IPOs/mid-caps are not discovered until manually killed and rerun.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap fetchScreener/fetchExchangePage in a per-call timeout (race a setTimeout reject) and parallelize the region x bucket sweep with a bounded worker pool (4-6 concurrent), keeping the sleep as the rate governor.

findings.title: fetchScreener documents 'retry up to 3 times' but only backs off twice (off-by-one)
findings.description: fetchScreener loops attempt 0..2 (3 iterations) but the 429 retry guard is `is429 && attempt < 2`, so it backs off+continues only after attempts 0 and 1. A 429 on the final attempt (2) fails the guard, falls through the catch, and returns [] — no third retry. The comment claims 'retry up to 3 times on 429'; actual behavior is 'try up to 3 times, retry-with-backoff only twice'. A sustained 429 that a third backoff would clear silently drops that region/bucket's tickers.
findings.mechanism: The retry guard attempt<2 combined with a 0..2 loop yields 3 attempts but only 2 backoff-retries; a 429 on the last attempt returns [] without the documented third retry.
findings.reproducer: Make yf.screener 429 three times; observe only two 5s/10s backoffs then an empty [] return rather than a third retry — the bucket contributes zero tickers.
findings.impact: Occasional silent loss of one region/bucket's tickers under sustained 429; minor because buckets overlap, but coverage is measured against the shrunken set with no attributable signal.
findings.suggested_fix: Align code with intent (retry on the last attempt too) or fix the comment to 'up to 2 retries'; add a warn distinguishing 429-exhausted from other failures so coverage shrink is attributable.

findings.title: price-only floor skips when quote omits marketCap; decayed sub-$1B names linger
findings.description: In _priceOnlyUpdate, existing.marketCap.value is only updated when q.marketCap != null (line 1570), and the MIN_MCAP floor only acts when mcapNow != null && mcapNow < MIN_MCAP (line 1580). If yf.quote() returns no marketCap (common for thin/illiquid and some intl venues), the snapshot retains the PREVIOUS full-pull marketCap and the floor is evaluated against that stale value. Because the price-only fast path keeps meta.asOf young (<7d), a full pull that would recompute mcap never triggers — so a stock that has since collapsed below $1B but whose quote omits marketCap stays in the universe indefinitely. The full-pull path explicitly treats mcapMissing as below-floor (lines 1989-1991), but the price-only path does not mirror that null-as-below-floor rule.
findings.mechanism: price-only refreshes mcap only when the quote provides it; a missing q.marketCap leaves stale mcap in place, the floor passes on stale data, and the young asOf prevents a corrective full pull, so a decayed sub-floor ticker persists.
findings.reproducer: Take a ~$1B ticker whose yf.quote() omits marketCap; run repeated daily price-only refreshes — it never drops below the floor check even after a real decline because mcap is never re-evaluated and a full pull is never forced.
findings.impact: Small-cap survivor bias inconsistent with the full-pull floor: decayed names linger in the scored universe, distorting universe composition over time.
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the full-pull rule: if q.marketCap is null in price-only (for USD-trading tickers), force a full pull or mark the stale mcap untrusted so the next cycle re-evaluates it.

findings.title: Quarterly series order assumed (QS latest-first, FTS reverse) with no date-based guard
findings.description: The mapper asserts the legacy quoteSummary quarterly array is latest-first ('Engine erwartet latest=index 0') and the FTS path explicitly slice().reverse() to convert oldest->latest. Neither validates the rows' own period/endDate before relying on the order. Since legacy QS quarterly data is mostly empty (F-DP-003), the live exposure is the FTS slice().reverse() assumption: there is no assertion that fts.quarterlyFin actually arrives oldest-first. If Yahoo ever flips FTS quarterly ordering, the reverse inverts every quarterly series and the same-quarter-YoY logic in downstream methods (qRev[i] vs qRev[i+4]) silently compares the wrong quarters with no error.
findings.mechanism: Quarterly array ordering is assumed and never validated against the rows' period/date fields, so an upstream ordering flip silently produces reversed series and wrong-quarter YoY math.
findings.reproducer: Feed an FTS quarterly fixture already in latest-first order; slice().reverse() makes it oldest-first and revenue-acceleration-yoy compares q[0] (now oldest) against q[4] — wrong sign/magnitude, no error.
findings.impact: If Yahoo flips quarterly ordering, every quarterly-derived signal (acceleration, deceleration-guard, single-quarter-dependency) silently inverts across the universe — low probability, high blast radius, undetectable without a guard.
findings.suggested_fix: Sort each quarterly array by the rows' period/endDate descending explicitly instead of trusting array order; assert/log if the incoming order disagreed.

findings.title: refresh-universe rewrites watchlist + fresh timestamp even on a Yahoo-side blackout
findings.description: main() is purely additive: it accumulates allTickers from screeners + exchanges + discovery, pushes only new tickers, never removes existing ones, then unconditionally writes watchlist.json and stamps lastUniverseRefresh fresh. There is no floor on how many SOURCES actually succeeded. If every Yahoo screener AND every exchange page 429'd (returning [] / error) and only the auth-free discovery sources contributed, the watchlist is still rewritten with a fresh timestamp — a degraded refresh looks identical to a healthy one in the committed artifact. The per-exchange zero-quote warning (line 310) and screener WARN logs exist but nothing aggregates 'Yahoo screener contributed N of expected hundreds' into a gate or non-zero exit.
findings.mechanism: The refresh unconditionally rewrites the watchlist with a fresh timestamp regardless of how many discovery sources succeeded, so a Yahoo-side blackout is invisible in the output artifact and timestamp.
findings.reproducer: Force all fetchScreener/fetchExchangePage to fail; refresh still writes watchlist.json with lastUniverseRefresh bumped and new-ticker count from discovery only, no failure signal.
findings.impact: Silent degradation of universe growth: newly-IPO'd / grown mid-caps that only Yahoo screeners surface are missed, but the run reports success; over repeated degraded runs the universe stagnates undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: Track contribution counts per source class (screener, exchange, discovery); if Yahoo screener+exchange contribution is zero (or below a floor) while discovery succeeded, emit ::warning:: or exit non-zero so CI flags the partial refresh.
